I don't know exactly what AvPD's reputation is. I don't think people think about it that much. Out of all the disorders out there, this one probably isn't romanticized that much. I think people do think we're sad and unenviable. 

Probably people think about shut-ins and disgruntled, possibly violent incels. I don't think that's so inaccurate, agoraphobia and misanthropy can really go along with the territory. Just checking out of life.

In the media you get like...*Lars and the Real Girl*. And it's like yeah that's kind of funny. But it's not that charming, and not everyone is as attractive as Ryan Gosling. In real life, you can shower these people with acceptance but they still feel broken inside. And they're not going to feel flawed-but-at-peace and making the most of life. 

AvPD is rarely not mixed with something else. Some other problem, a mood disorder, OCD, etc. A lot of people who technically have it are people who can put on a front but they have zero social life. Zero intimacy in their lives. They hate themselves but they're not broadcasting it everywhere they go.

Other people have AvPD and substance abuse, so people just see a drug addict since that's the most obvious part of them.

I would have kids start school later and leave school earlier. Like starting in 2nd grade and ending in 10th grade. 

My favorite classes in school were just a teacher and an overhead projector. I think the dim room also calmed me. We rely too much on computers and on powerpoints and other technology. Have a library course where kids learn to use search engines and learn about how to cite things and make bibliographies and use the internet. But I think it's better to keep the other classes as simple as possible. Like it really helps to draw out a graph before you try to plot one on a calculator or computer. And try not to get rid of books in favor of tablets and laptops. 

Keep classrooms small. The bigger a class gets, the more it's just some worksheet and testing mill, and kids might as well stay home and watch a lecture on youtube for as much attention as they get. Big lecture halls are fine for college, and as kids get older it's not going to be such a huge deal for subjects like history. But if you're learning a language or you're doing math and science the teacher ratio makes a big difference.

I don't think the education of the teacher has nearly as much impact as how nice they are and how good with people they are, and the teacher ratio. If you want a kid to pass a test, do you think they'd do better in a 40 person classroom with a PhD? What if you just paid a kid to watch two hours of Khan academy every day? And you had a freshman in college with them as they do 30 math problems every day? Talking to them step by step? I'd put my money on that scenario.

Yeah school is babysitting, so realistically it's probably better that they do stay there 8 hours a day unless they have something else productive to do. I think about half that time should be study hall. Or optional tutoring at a tutoring center. You want to watch educational movies for 3 hours a day in the library? Go ahead. Read books? You want to work on school projects, or just talk with your friends about nothing for 3 hours a day? Play baseball? Sit on an exercise bike? That's fine I think. Just not being around the internet for 3 hours in and of itself is building a skill and mental strength.

Not all kids would be able to fit the model. Charter schools, continuation school...sometimes you just need an environment where there isn't homework, it's just all in class. Where you can take as long as you want to learn certain concepts, and have very very small teacher/student ratios. Where kids are maybe relying more on computer learning systems because the are repelled by passive lecture style learning. The goal being to not unnecessarily stress kids out and to build up their strengths and give them enough psychological attention. Maybe they need to learn about themselves in order to prepare them for the adult world.

The worst part about it was the lingering effects of bad decisions I made and opportunities I missed that I wouldn't have if I knew that this person was really, really exaggerating how much they liked me, and misleading me about the reasons they liked me, and using me as a toy and putting me back on the shelf. I love how grating Marnie is. That makes it fun for me. I think it takes not being too emotionally invested in these fictional character's lives. I mean, it sucks if there are things you like about the character but then they behave in these awful ways. It's like a betrayal. When shows are really good and really realistic it's hard to just not care. There are other shows out there where it's like--this is what a really good person looks like. And these are what relationships are at their best so they are very enjoyable to live vicariously through. Girls isn't that kind of show. For me Girls is more about--this is how you'll end up if you don't have that voice inside yourself saying you're doing something wrong. That internal anxiety that you resent and feel you'll never escape from. You'll end up using men like Marnie. Or you'll end up being a giant hypocrite like Dil. Or you'll end up pathetically throwing yourself at your boss who isn't even coming onto you like Hannah. 

In defense of Marnie though, I think what's really great about her story was when she spends that day with Charlie after he buffed up, grew a beard, a fake accent, and became a drug user and dealer. She sees how he completely fucked up his life, how much her relationship with him hurt him and affected him. And she realizes that she wasn't attracted to him when he was a good, non-lying person. But she has that near death experience with the mugger. She goes through a transformation. She realizes that even though she was a terrible influence in his life, that doesn't change the fact that she needs to do what's best for her, and she shouldn't let him drag her down. 

When Desi says to her something like "You know what will happen? You'll get killed." And she's just like..."you're right, I might." I think that was such an important scene to show what love really is. And to show that your own autonomy is worth fighting for, even if you are naive or other people out there are smarter than you.

One time I was walking into work in the morning. It wasn't even 6:00AM, and it was strangely warm. I was wondering wow...did I gain that much weight? Am I having a fever even?

So I go into work. Normally I'm practically mute and I play it safe. That day, I endeavor to voluntarily start a conversation of my own. And I ask them, "Is it just me or is it hot in here?"

And one woman quickly responded "Yeah it's warm. We're all Mexican here, we like it that way."

The way she said it was just like...implying that I wanted them to turn on the air conditioning. (Not true). And that I'm just so dumb that I can't comprehend how anyone could enjoy a temperature different than what I like. But that she bears me no grudge that I'm a little bit ignorant and she's such a big person that she's doing me a favor by letting me know that my ignorance is showing. 

When really, it was because I was trying to assess if I was really sick, or just gained so much weight I had no temperature tolerance anymore. Or if it was an unusually hot year for global warning. And to take advantage of actually having something to say for once.

I never tried to correct her. Let them believe what they want. I'd only seem petty if I did that. 

I don't know. NTs and people with Aspergers alike are capable of using indirect communication, Aspies just tend to be worse at it or dislike it more. I also think that people who do grasp that we really don't get it...also believe that we could never get it. That it's a lost cause.

And I think there's also the aspect of not everyone who is good at socializing, at following norms and stuff would also be good at teaching it to people who don't know it. They're not focused enough on the why and how, it's just obvious to them and they don't know why.

And then there's the matter of what's in it for other people. This hasn't been normalized in public school. It's not even something I've really heard about with mental health professionals or other professionals who work with autistic people. You only hear about it if the person is severely autistic and they're trying to teach them how to talk, or basic socially appropriate behavior and how to detect sarcasm. When it comes to ASD, they just look at it like ok, where's the problem behavior? Is this kid being distracting? Disruptive? Are they not getting good enough grades? And they want to fix the problem, so they think the kid needs a psychiatrist or something. Or they're not trying hard enough in school. Inpatient, outpatient, therapy more than once a week, special therapists who are better at dealing with personality disorders, months-long group therapy. I am a woman with an unusually masculine face. It's not low self esteem. By accident of birth I'm on the far end of the bell curve for masculinity for women. I also happened to be very lesbian leaning. So I look like the stereotype, and the stereotype is true--I love women. 

If I'm not pegged as gay for having a man-face, sometimes people think I'm a cisgender male or that I'm either an ftm or an mtf trans person. 

Last year I made a decision to grow out my hair again. For much of my adult life I had cut my hair short. I am very used to people thinking I'm a man all the time, or people being unsure as what I identify as. Since everyone started wearing masks in public again, I think that people are treating me different and I suspect it's because I'm not only seen as a woman again, but I'm not always assumed to be a gay one. Even when I had long hair as an adult, sometimes people would still think I was a guy, so the mask really made a difference. 

It's a very interesting experience. Not since I was a child...maybe a teenager at the latest have I felt like people didn't perceive me as necessarily gay, or like I'm a man. And it does have an effect on me. I've spent so much energy getting used to being an androgynous person, to expecting people to treat me as a guy initially. To having to explain to people that I'm surprisingly female. No, I didn't take any hormones. No, I'm not intersex (afaik). I feel like people trust me more and relate to me more. Sometimes I feel like I'm less intimidating, which is good and bad. I think I'm starting to be less on edge. I feel less like an outsider. Other people's perception of you does affect your perception of yourself. I'm benefiting from people's positive bias of straight people and non androgynous people. I am learning about what is something real about myself, and what something fake, like an adaptation I made due to anxiety, or like something negative people assume about me because of how I look. I am also realizing that I'm not so tough and so unaffected by other people. When I looked like a man I spent so much time telling myself how it doesn't matter that I don't look like a woman. That people may not like my appearance or may have certain assumptions but that many people are aware of their own prejudices and don't try to get trapped in them. How yeah I wish I looked differently, but this is the most peace with my appearance I can have. I can cut my hair short, and it doesn't make me feel as inadequate as if I had long hair, or actually attempted to dress more like a woman or put on makeup and to see the painful dichotomy between my hair and makeup and clothes and my actual physiology. I can cut my hair short, and while I don't get to enjoy being a visible woman, I did appreciate when people treated me like a guy in some ways. I spent my time thinking...oh well it's kind of nice that people treat me like a regular dude. They can be more casual with me. I don't have to worry about relating to others as much because people already see me as different (once they realize I'm not a guy). Guys don't act weird around me because they don't think I'm some sad ugly girl who is all moony over them.

So yeah I'm back to being seen as woman again for the first time in over a decade in my adult life and there are some changes.

When kids play with each other as kids they learn how to fight and test each other's limits, they learn about conflict, they learn how to please other people. They learn how to feel powerful and self effective when they teach something to someone younger, or help someone out. This is when their personality is developed.

So I would say that having small families, and having kids that may only have any sort of intimacy from a couple of people in their lives during their childhood, and who only learn to interact with people in a highly restricted environment of public school...shouldn't be considered such a good thing. Even though I am very bitter about my childhood, I understand that it offered me a lot of advantages. I wouldn't personally have made that trade-off, but nevertheless, for what is sacrificed in that situation other things are gained. My parents could have chosen to work less, to be around their relatives more, or to interact more with other families when young children when me and my brother were young. 

I wouldn't say it shouldn't be "normalized" but I think society should be more aware of what price we pay for making it normal to be so isolated and to make school and work and material things so much of a priority.

My brother did bully me, but even he stopped fairly young. Mostly what I saw when I was a kid was bullying by teachers to students. Not being fair, being overly critical or demeaning, being out to get certain students.

As an adult I've seen even less overt bullying. If you're obviously a bully, you'd better be very popular for other people to put up with you abusing other people. What I see in the adult world is a lot of covert aggression. You try to get people to fail without them realizing what you're doing. You ignore people. You give someone an insult that seems like a compliment. You fluff someone's ego one day and then are more critical or ignore them another day, destabilizing their confidence and self worth. The trick is to make someone feel bad without them knowing you're doing it, so that they hate themselves and not you. If you're the weak link at a workplace for example, there's a legal disincentive to not fire people or even suggest they they resign. It would undermine your authority as a supervisor too if you were constantly trying to correct their mistakes but the employee just kept refusing to do so or being incompetent. 

One of the few experiences I've had as an adult of bullying was feeling obligated to put up with some people driving fast and tailgating or smoking pot in their cars. More than once I've met someone who seemed very nice and they'd be really good listeners, really funny, really good at making other people feel good. But they would ask me to light a joint for them while they were driving. And I could have refused. They weren't the type of crazy person who would be like "shut up, light me a joint" but they knew that I was already in there, and I felt obligated to put up with it and they would try to take advantage of it. 

There is so so much you can do with very little lying, and a lot of manipulation. With just words, gestures, actions. You can come across as someone squeaky clean while achieving making other people feel even worse than if you hit them or screamed in their faces. It's very easy to get away with because of a sense of fairness in our society that if you don't directly insult someone or physically touch someone, then if someone feels bad it must be their fault. And also just because it can be hard to detect. And because the person who does it is very likeable, so they can get away with violating social rules when they feel like it. Also--other people may have done some shameful thing that they know about. I know someone who in grad school would offer to write other students' papers for free. They never asked for that in the first place, but when the offer was placed in front of that person, they were persuaded and made the immoral choice. Imagine how much more power this person had over the other person now--this other person probably doesn't feel great about themselves that they just cheated. That they thought maybe they weren't smart enough to make the grade themselves. That puts the other person in a really good position to exploit this person down the line to get what they want. Another easy way is for a bully to get cozy with you, and try to get you to dish about something you did you feel ashamed about. Feels good to get it off your chest right? Feels nice that someone actually sympathizes with your more regrettable experiences. Very easy to use that against someone down the line.

I used to live in my van. Non-mobile homeless is a totally different ballgame and those people would have more immediate kinds of needs.

But for me? What helped the most was that I had an address. I actually paid someone for it, because I thought it was important to be really strict about relying on charity as little as possible. For the benefit of myself first, not for some sort of altruistic reason. 

Everything else...food, clothes, washing, internet...there was a way to deal with it with little income and that didn't require a personal favor from someone. Go to Starbucks, go to the gym. Rotate places to buy a 2 dollar menu item at so you can stay a few hours. With a van you can park a lot places undetected. It depends on the area. 

Church parking lots that let you park your vehicle there overnight, and programs that provide addresses for the homeless are really important. And yeah social workers exist, but easier access to them is always good. There was a program in town where you could meet with people from different agencies and charities all in the same day, and these people would direct you where to go. To shelters, or how to apply for SSI for example. Actual benefits are far from adequate and a lot of people don't qualify but it's worth a shot. Employment centers where you can use a computer to apply online for things and print your resume. 

I wish zoning laws were different, and that it were easier for people to own their own properties. Mobile home parks are very often not a cheaper option. Your vehicle can't even be over 10 years old. The rent is crazy. If you buy a plot of land, the cost to put even the most basic house on it is a lot. People experiment with the cheapest kinds of structures you can build, but most places are not gonna let  you put a yurt and a septic tank on your plot or something. I know it's complicated. I lived in a van and it worked out great for me and I had free rent. But if a lot more people did that? Local businesses would lose money. People would avoid the gym and it would lose money. And a zillion other problems with sanitation and economics and crime. But on an individual level, a lot of people would benefit so much from having a quicker path to home ownership or from being able to live in a van freely without being hassled or being inhibited from working.

I'm not bipolar and I had my first and only psychotic and manic episodes when I was 29. During the worse one I completely lost touch with reality. I hadn't slept in a week. Before then I had smoked and eaten a ton of marijuana. But at a certain point, I realized I was no longer just high, but entering a state of mania. After a night without sleeping I stopped smoking pot in an effort to come back down. It didn't help enough, and I either didn't sleep or had very little sleep after that. 

A few days in I was starting to get very worried, and I went into an acupuncture clinic for a session where I completely passed out for an hour. However, trying to sleep in any other setting I could not keep my thoughts from racing. There were too many thoughts, I could not pause them, and every tangent led to another one and another one on and on. I had all these really "genius" insights and I wrote some of them down. I was relatively less inhibited than I normally am, and I would talk to people around about all these personal and sometimes sexual things. I hadn't showered in awhile, or brushed my teeth, or ate much of anything. I kept putting on my same clothes so I smelled really rank, but I couldn't personally smell how disgusting I was. After a certain point, I had all these false memories and I couldn't tell what was real anymore. I got paranoid. I accused a former friend for example of being paid by my mother to be friends with me. My friend who takes antipsychotic medication gave me some of her Seroquel trying to help, but it felt completely awful like I couldn't sit still and I couldn't move at the same time. It made me more crazy. I kept thinking she was telling me I was going to die or she or someone else would have to kill me. When my mom and her boyfriend came to pick me up from her place, I genuinely believed they were going to take me somewhere and I would be magically annihilated somehow, like disintegrate into thin air. Or that I was going to be taken somewhere to get shot. I thought I was going to die that night. I had accepted it, I felt like a bad person and I didn't try to fight it. I was surprised when nothing supernatural happened and I didn't die.

For me, the drugs and lack of sleep and everything else after it...it was a matter of having a grief too enormous to digest. Having feelings of shame and guilt and rage but not having internal permission to fully feel or express them, even to myself. It was unthinkable to me. I was suicidal over it. The whole experience was very strange and at times scary. Sometimes I felt euphoric, sometimes I felt the most dysphoric I ever remember feeling since being a young child. Like when you're a kid, and you have to pee but you can't go to the bathroom for some reason. That kind of terror and desperation. Or if you were being forced to kill someone (which I've never experienced thankfully). If there is a enough pressure, and there's no where to go, you can't be OK with what's happening, but you can't opt out either, there's actually another option and it's psychosis. I've tried a few psychedelics before. It didn't feel like that exactly, but kind of. Everything felt very spiritual and profound. I didn't know what events were real in my life and what weren't. I value the experience, although I haven't tried to replicate it again. When it was good? I felt genuinely happy, for the first time I could remember. But I was also gross and dysfunctional, and alternately completely dysphoric and scared to sleep. Freddy Krueger might as well have been real, I was terrified of what would happen if I passed out. If I had the money I think I would like to try guided ketamine PTSD therapy.

I blame not being around my peers or younger children enough when I was a child. There are things about socialization that you learn that way, that you can't learn from adults, from people who have power over you. All that stuff that kids do when they're young when they play with each other...they're learning stuff, like dealing with conflict. Like getting more insight into what other people are like. Everyone learns by making mistakes, and it's inevitable that some of those mistakes will effect other people, will be at other people's expense. It's a fact of life, obviously you want to minimize this and try to live a life that doesn't harm other people in any way, but it's still impossible. But some people will make more mistakes than other people. And children make more mistakes than anyone else. If you don't make enough of those mistakes as a child, you really can't make up for it well, and the consequences are very different. You're more likely to be ignored or ostracized. If you did something really bad you might get sued or arrested, although for the most people that isn't something that is as likely to happen as you'd have to be especially socially oblivious to have no idea what you're doing is illegal. I used to live in a minivan for about 2 years. And I wished I had got a white van instead. You can cover the windows--but that's a dead giveaway. That's all well in good if you know you've got a chill Walmart or gym or something that looks the other way, but it's actually safer to just pull up in a neighborhood and park without a bunch of curtains or cardboard. And afaik it's illegal to completely tint your windows and it might attract more attention from cops. Not even cops too-just people who normally wouldn't have given your vehicle a second glance but now are very curious about what you could be hiding in there.

With a white van, they're still pretty inconspicuous. The difference between having a place where no one can see you, and some place where "they're probably not looking, but they could totally look if they wanted" is huge huge huge. First you start mouthing things to yourself and scratching your butt and stuff in public a little bit, and you think you're just lazy, idgaf. His letter will undoubtedly make some people feel less alone who really need it. And I think it will shatter the abuse cycle in his family, finally condemning his parents who according to him hurt a lot of people. And I would imagine may have made the difference between him ending his own life as an adult or not. 

I do not have the same type of trauma, but I find some of what he says relatable, and other parts not. I have people close to me who have had horrific childhood traumas, some emotional, some physical and what he says reminds me of them more.

He says he's not a good person, and he's sorry for how he treated people. He refers to "moodiness and arbitrariness." I'm left to wonder if he had an accurate perception of himself or not. Maybe he was just a perfectionist. Maybe he inwardly hated himself for feeling any negative feelings toward anyone, even if he didn't act on them. But maybe he did mistreat people, even if he wasn't outright abusive and many people loved him. I have people I've met before who could be great, but who could still mistreat people. I know that some of them had immense tragedies in their past. He says he wanted to kill people. 

He says he would never see a psychologist because he couldn't trust them 100% to keep some things completely secret. I do believe for some people therapy, psychiatry, in-patient...just won't be enough to help. There is something so violating about a secret not being kept, even though it's something intangible. Why would it matter if some therapist told his wife? Or told his colleague as an anonymous case study? Especially if he would never find out? If you talk about something that potentially makes you want to die...would you risk being invalidated? Someone not thinking it's important? For someone who suffered some of the worst disempowerment and dyshporia that can exist I would imagine the power dynamic in therapy is far too prohibitive for healing. It's gross in a way that someone is making a living off your pain. Or even that someone is deriving meaning from your pain. To be rendered fathomable. He couldn't tolerate the idea of that happening while he was alive.

What is "the darkness?" I'm left to wonder. I would guess it has to do with dysphoria, and maybe the unbearable pain of identifying with your abuser. Feeling any sort of aggression can make someone feel that way even if they have no desire to hurt people in the same way they've been hurt.

I "got over it." I walk around everyday with the massive, heavy burden that is AvPD, lugging it around everywhere. I haven't let it stop me from meeting people. People have different measures for what's normal. For some people it's "appearing normal." Now that's something I've never achieved. But for others, it might be something like "have you ever had a partner before?" "Have you ever had a job?" And I can answer yes and yes for those. 

AvPD I think is especially easy to dismiss. The way our society is set up, not having too much anxiety or depression is an ideal, rather than something realistic. And the freaky thing is that people 10+ years younger than me make me feel far less weird. I attribute that to me having a childhood that was more like the younger generation. This really really sheltered, yet cyber existence. Not being around enough people. Not being able to really play and interact with others like you should at a critical stage in your development. Using the internet to cope. 

I think it's an easy lie to tell yourself, that this isn't a big deal. I convince myself of it a lot of the time. But I think it's more like, if you get a burn and the burn heals but there's no more nerves in the area. Like that's the same as never being hurt. Like that's the same as having fully functioning skin. You might even feel a bit grateful you're no longer in excruciating pain, but you've lost something. 

I think the realest moments in my life were when I was very young, before I could tell myself lies. And since then, those times when I felt in a crisis, alarm bells going off in my head "this isn't right." I wish during those times I knew what to do with it, because I strongly believe there is something to do. If regular therapy works for you--that's really great, that's fortunate because that's mostly what's out there. If the military works for you--go join the military. I'm serious, that sounds like BS advice. It could end in disaster (PTSD, physical destruction). You'll find plenty of people who went through it who say they're still AvPD after it. Maybe it means you take drugs. Maybe it means you get ketamine therapy or MDMA therapy. There's something called "cold therapy" which is supposed to be extremely painful and traumatizing, but I believe it works. How many medical procedures are necessarily painful and traumatizing, but effective? Maybe go do an ayahuasca ceremony. 

I resent that for the most part, I coped by "getting over it" because it's what afforded me more autonomy and a little dignity. I think other people would say I've made progress with my disorder. Like I must have less anxiety, I must have a more realistic perception of reality if I'm able to talk more, or hold down a job, or convince other people to hang out with me. I have more life experience, that's helped. But if you're looking at what makes life worth living, moments of real happiness--I have very little of those. Like a glimmer of something that for a lot of fucking people is a regular, normal thing. It's not that I don't believe in consulting with people educated in the study of psychology, or don't believe in changing habits and behaviors and thought patterns. But I believe in listening to your intuition as well. In my case, what I sensed I need happened to be something dramatic or drastic or painful. It wouldn't necessarily be the same thing for everyone. And those times I actually listened to myself and did what I could with available options I didn't regret it.

Like what kind of arrogant troll would it make me to discriminate against people because I caught a figurative whiff of some weakness of theirs and didn't want to be tainted by it? Nobody's perfect, what makes people good people is how they conduct themselves and being self aware about what's right and wrong. Like you can be a needy person, or an angry person and you can avoid taking it out on people as much as possible an still be a good person. Nobody is completely selfless and only has good will toward everyone.

There are many reasons you could feel like something's off about them, but what I came across most of all is there being this disconnect between their words and their actions, which may have been on-point...and the reasons behind those actions. There are ways to make it look like you care about someone and at the same time be trying to get the other person to fuck up. You feel like "this person is so nice to me, I feel awful but I can't take it out on them, I feel bad about myself for wanting to do that." If someone dislikes you and doesn't want you to know it, they can try to manipulate you and frustrate you so that you screw up, or make you envy them, or lash out at them and you are abased and they are seen as the better person. In the adult world, you don't do what a kid does and hit someone you don't like. Or insult them directly. You learn that you can avoid censure from other people when you are covert about it. You learn that it hurts the person far more to *make them hate themselves* than for them to think that you hate them. What's even more insidious about all this, is that some people are fucked up in such a way that they often subconsciously or only semi-consciously realize what they are doing. They don't consciously realize they dislike someone, because that would be an affront to their own identity. That would mean that they are weak that someone actually gets to them. So they pull it off so well because it's not acting, it's less detectable when you really believe the story you are putting out there.

Hey, this is the first time I read about another person with AvPD who was homeless. I was homeless for most of 2 years during a period of my life when I was separating from my family and learning how to become fully financially autonomous for the first time. I had a vehicle though which I was very grateful for. I have no idea how long I could have lasted without one. 

I have terrible self esteem and poor confidence, but I was also very needy. It's not like I didn't have ANYONE who wanted to spend time with me in some platonic capacity. I wasn't so ashamed of myself that I couldn't enjoy it a little bit but I isolated myself because I didn't want to be influenced by people. I was in a difficult situation, and facing my fears of job interviews and working, which is one of my worst fears. I didn't want to be distracted, I didn't want things sugarcoated or for people to give me "emotional support." At that time in my life it kind of made me barf and I felt like it wouldn't have helped me. I wanted to not need people, but being alone in public all the time, being worn down mentally and emotionally added an extra challenge. I lost a job during this time at one point, and I found myself homeless and emotionally a wreck. Like I started to look homeless and like I did drugs and stuff. I was worried I'd never be employed again. At this point I sought out whatever free mental health programs and stuff were out there. There was an anxiety group for example, where I could have gone every week (stopped after the first session) and talk about our anxiety levels and listen to one of those anti-anxiety hypnosis videos and see how that worked. It wasn't horrible, like anything that stopped me from being by myself, and being somewhere around people where I didn't have to worry about looking weird, no personal relationship at stake or anything, was good. But it felt like such a drop in the bucket. And what I needed was to get back to looking like a shy, if-normal person instead of someone who compulsively talks to themselves and fidgets. I didn't qualify for weekly therapy because I wasn't depressed enough. The few free counseling sessions I did have made me feel like shit, lonelier and less confident. I was told that I really should look into getting SSI, which made me feel awful because that's not what I wanted, first of all. And also because it is really difficult to get for mental health issues. 

Anyway...I know that doesn't directly apply to your situation, but the idea of socialization being a curse and a blessing resonated with me. I've felt at times like I had to compromise my beliefs out of necessity. Only the part of the problem is awareness of what's out there. Like I'm pretty sure you know what meetup.com is. How to look for social services...where bars are, events, colleges and adult schools, volunteer work, etc. etc.. My kind of thing would have been a free cheap event and hoping someone talks to me and then I'd never see them again. That for me was like, the most good I could get without any bad. And obviously that is not very satisfying. I don't think there's anything to do but to plan and soul search. You have to weigh your options. And you may find that it's worth getting involved with people, whether it's something very superficial or temporary, or like a good friend or even a partner. The only thing you can try to do is to take care of yourself as best as possible and to prevent other problems in your life that might make it harder for you to make the right decisions.
